articles.title: Tiered administration remains the weak point in Active Directory estates
articles.author: tomas-reyes
articles.summary: Incident responders say most directory compromises still involve privileged credentials exposed on lower-tier systems.
articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for infrastructure story: Active Directory

brief.what: Incident responders say most directory compromises still involve privileged credentials exposed on lower-tier systems.
brief.who: Organisations without privileged access workstations remain particularly exposed.
brief.why: Estates without privileged access workstations or credential isolation remain at significant risk.
brief.next: Expect auditors to ask for evidence of tiering and delegation reviews.

articles.whyItMatters: Estates without privileged access workstations or credential isolation remain at significant risk. Implement tiering, restrict where privileged accounts can sign in, and audit delegation regularly.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Incident responders say most directory compromises still involve privileged credentials exposed on lower-tier systems.
Delegation left over from past projects often grants broader rights than intended.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Tiered administration separates control of domain controllers from ordinary servers and workstations.
Most domain compromises still follow credential exposure on lower-tier systems followed by privilege escalation.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Estates without privileged access workstations or credential isolation remain at significant risk.
Organisations without privileged access workstations remain particularly exposed.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Implement tiering, restrict where privileged accounts can sign in, and audit delegation regularly.
Expect auditors to ask for evidence of tiering and delegation reviews.

articles.author: tomas-reyes
articles.summary: Updated regulatory guidance asks financial institutions to evidence periodic restore tests.
articles.imageAlt: Editorial illustration for infrastructure story: Backup

brief.what: Updated regulatory guidance asks financial institutions to evidence periodic restore tests.
brief.who: Financial institutions and their IT providers need documented restore results.
brief.why: Financial institutions and critical service providers face the most direct requirements.
brief.next: Guidance takes effect after a transition period.

articles.whyItMatters: Financial institutions and critical service providers face the most direct requirements. Schedule automated restore tests, keep immutable copies and document recovery time results.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Updated regulatory guidance asks financial institutions to evidence periodic restore tests.
Successful backup jobs alone will no longer be sufficient evidence of recoverability.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Backups are only useful if they can be restored; untested backups frequently fail during real incidents.
Regulators and auditors increasingly ask for evidence of periodic restore testing, not only backup job success.

sections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Financial institutions and critical service providers face the most direct requirements.
Financial institutions and their IT providers need documented restore results.

sections.heading: What you should know
paragraphs: Schedule automated restore tests, keep immutable copies and document recovery time results.
Guidance takes effect after a transition period.

brief.what: Operations teams are replacing per-host threshold alerts with alerts tied to service level objectives.
brief.who: On-call engineers report fewer but more actionable pages.

brief.next: Expect monitoring tools to ship more SLO features by default.

articles.whyItMatters: On-call teams typically see fewer but more actionable alerts after migration. Start with a few critical user journeys, define SLIs carefully and review alert quality after each incident.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Operations teams are replacing per-host threshold alerts with alerts tied to service level objectives.
Burn-rate alerts catch sustained degradation while ignoring brief spikes.

sections.heading: Technical Analysis
paragraphs: Service level objectives define reliability targets from the user's perspective rather than per-host thresholds.
Alerting on error-budget burn rates reduces noisy pages while catching sustained degradation.

sections.heading: What you should know
